resources.string: Used to capture screenshots via Quick Settings tile
SnapTile uses an accessibility service only to take screenshots when you tap the Quick Settings tile. No other data is collected.
SnapTile takes screenshots cleanly via an accessibility service (no screen-recording prompt). Turn it on once under Accessibility → SnapTile.
Turn off for banking / UPI apps

Bank and UPI apps warn about any enabled third-party accessibility service, even one like SnapTile that only takes screenshots. It is now off, so those warnings stop. The tile still captures — Android asks for screen-capture consent each time. Turn it back on above for prompt-free capture.
Accessibility turned off. Re-enable it any time from this screen.
Turn SnapTile off under Accessibility settings

Tap the tile and the shot is taken at once — no prompt and no consent dialog. Full-screen shots are saved by Android itself; region and paint go through Android\'s screen-recording consent. Needs SnapTile\'s accessibility service switched on — and banks and UPI apps warn about any enabled accessibility service, so they will warn about this one.

Android\'s own capture consent, the way any screen recorder works. No accessibility service is needed, so banking and UPI apps stay quiet. Android asks before each capture, so it is one extra tap every time.
Legacy method on. SnapTile\'s accessibility service is now off, so banking and UPI apps stop warning.
Native method on. Turn on SnapTile\'s accessibility service to use it.

SnapTile\'s accessibility service is what the native method captures through, and only you can switch it on — Android never lets an app enable it for itself. For an app installed outside a store there is one extra step in front of that, so do these in order.

SnapTile captures through an accessibility service so it can take the shot without Android\'s screen-recording prompt. That service has to be switched on by you — Android does not allow an app to enable it for itself.
SnapTile\'s accessibility service is off, so the native method cannot capture yet. Turn it on below — start at step 1 — or switch SnapTile to the Legacy method on the main screen.
SnapTile\'s accessibility service is on ✓ — the native method is ready.
If the SnapTile switch is greyed out

On Android 13 and newer, Android hides this switch for apps installed outside a store — Android\'s rule for side-loaded apps, not something SnapTile can ask for at install time. The order below matters: the “Allow restricted settings” row only appears in the App info menu after you have tried the greyed-out switch once and been refused, which is why this screen starts in Accessibility settings rather than in App info.

Tap 1 · OPEN ACCESSIBILITY SETTINGS below, then tap SNAPTILE in the list. The switch there is greyed out and Android tells you a restricted setting is blocking it. That is expected, and making the attempt is what unlocks step 2.
Tap 2 · OPEN APP INFO below — that is SnapTile\'s App info page — then ⋮ at the top right, then “Allow restricted settings”.
Tap 1 again to reopen Accessibility settings, tap SNAPTILE, and turn the switch on. It is live now, and it stays on.
STEP 2 IN DETAIL — TAP 1, THEN TAP 2
